title: From a measured surface to a usable asset

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Imagine scanning a metal surface so finely that you can see every scratch as a tiny hill or valley. What do you do with all those heights?

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Look at them, I suppose. Maybe turn them into a 3D model.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Both, and that's TrueMapData. This Python library reads surface captures from TrueMap and GelSight, exposes their heights as NumPy arrays, and gives you tools for analysis and graphics export from the same representation.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: What's inside one of these capture files?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: A dot t m d file holds a header, spatial metadata and a grid of heights stored as float32 values, row by row. It reads both the older v1 format and the TrueMap v6-style v2 format. The metadata keeps the physical scan size, so the grid never loses its real-world scale.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So it's like a topographic map of a tiny patch of material.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Exactly that. And you can explore it: a 2D heatmap, a 3D surface, row and column profiles, contour lines, and comparisons between files. Matplotlib makes static plots, Plotly saves an interactive HTML view, and optional Polyscope opens a 3D inspection window.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Then where do the graphics assets come in?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: From the same height grid, it derives normal maps, which describe local orientation for lighting, and displacement maps, which carry the height itself. It can also export meshes in formats like STL, OBJ, glTF and USD, and apply textures to a template model using the scan's millimeters per pixel to set the tiling.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Roughness analysis uses Surfalize for the ISO 25178 areal parameters. Wear analysis compares captures over time: it aligns frames with translation or OpenCV and SIFT registration, subtracts the heights, and reports volume loss, scratch evolution and roughness trajectories.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So one library, from raw scan to a game-ready mesh or a wear report.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Yes. The surface and profile figures in the post come from the project's own README examples. The full write-up has the diagram, the commands to try, and links to the guides.
